name: prips
desc: Print the IP addresses in a given range
why: Expands IP ranges into individual addresses, a tiny tool but a gentle entry point into CIDR arithmetic and address space.

brief.what_it_is: prips is a command-line tool that prints every IP address in a given range, one per line. You give it a start and end address, or a CIDR block like 192.168.0.0/24, and it outputs each address in turn. It can also go the other way with -c, turning a start and end address into a single CIDR block. The -i option sets the step between printed addresses, and -e excludes addresses from the output.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says prips "can enhance the usability of tools that are made to work on only one host at a time (e.g. whois)." It feeds address lists into single-host tools.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals beyond the examples. It shows that prips takes either a first and last address or a CIDR block and prints the addresses between them. Its output can be piped into a shell loop, as in the parallel ping example.

commands_seen.context: Example 1: prints every address from the start address to the end address, one per line.
Example 2: the same range given in CIDR notation.
Example 3: converts an IP range to CIDR notation; prints 192.168.0.0/28.
Example 4: -i sets the increment, so this prints only the network addresses of each /24 inside 10.8/16.
Example 5: -e excludes the last-octet 0 and 255 (network and broadcast) addresses, used inside a shell script that pings each host in parallel.
Install step: extracts the source tarball.
Install step: run inside the rust/ subdirectory; builds target/release/prips.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew is not the only route. The README's own instructions are: extract the source tarball, enter the rust/ subdirectory, run cargo build --release, then copy target/release/prips to a directory such as /usr/local/bin. That means a Rust toolchain is needed for a source build. The README gives no configuration or first-run steps.
brief.standout: The tool is tiny but does real address-space arithmetic, including converting a range back into CIDR. The README's parallel-ping script is a short shell pattern for sweeping a subnet using only prips and ping.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage shows a source tarball named prips-1.3.1 and a named maintainer, Peter Pentchev, but gives no release date, last commit, or changelog. I did not follow the GitLab or ReadTheDocs links, because the page text did not include their URLs.
brief.caveats: The README says it has only been tested on Linux and *BSD systems, and that it should work on any POSIX-compatible system. The Rust build is the documented route. The ping example is explicitly described as working only on small networks: it starts a process per host, and the README warns of a race that can hit the process limit. The README offers no license information on the page I read.
quotes: prips is a tool that can be used to print all of the IP address on a given range.
It can enhance the usability of tools that are made to work on only one host at a time (e.g. whois).
Note that this script only works on small networks because it uses a lot of processes.
